procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 06.03.2017 passed by the Rajasthan High Court in S.B. Criminal Misc. (Pet.) No. 3259 of 2015.

No. 3259 of 2015) filed under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, seeking to quash FIR No. 156 of 2015, Women Police Station, Udaipur, which alleged offences under Sections 498A, 406, 384, 420, and 120(B) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in not quashing FIR under Section 482 of Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 in a complaint alleging offences under Sections 498A, 406, 384, 420, and 120(B), Indian Penal Code, 1860, on the ground that the second FIR was on the same set of allegations.

facts: A complainant filed an FIR (No. 19 of 2015) in Hisar, Haryana, on October 17, 2015, under Section 498A IPC.

A few days later, on November 1, 2015, a second FIR (No. 156 of 2015) was registered in Udaipur, Rajasthan, based on a complaint filed by the same person on the same set of allegations, but with additional sections of the IPC.
The appellant filed a petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) before the Rajasthan High Court to quash the second FIR.
The High Court dismissed the petition, reasoning that the complaint in Udaipur was filed prior to the one in Hisar and that the Rajasthan Police were unaware of the first FIR.
law: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, a High Court has the inherent power to quash criminal proceedings to prevent an abuse of the process of law.
Filing a second FIR based on the same set of allegations as a previously filed FIR is considered an abuse of the process of law, especially if it appears intended to harass the accused.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's reasoning was factually incorrect and contradicted the record.
The record clearly showed that the complaint in Hisar was filed on October 10, 2015, five days before the complaint in Udaipur on October 15, 2015.

The Court also noted that the second complaint lodged in Udaipur explicitly mentioned the earlier complaint filed in Hisar, which disproved the High Court's finding that the Rajasthan Police were unaware of the first FIR.

The Supreme Court determined that the complainant's act of filing a second complaint in a different state on the same facts, without withdrawing the first or seeking its transfer, constituted a clear abuse of the legal process intended to harass the appellant.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court erred in dismissing the petition. It held that allowing the second FIR to proceed was an abuse of the process of law. Therefore, the Court accepted the appeal and quashed the second FIR registered in Udaipur, Rajasthan.

issue.issue_text: Non-application of mind by High Court – Findings of the High Court contradictory to the record and admitted facts.

facts: A criminal complaint (first FIR) was lodged against the appellant in Hisar.
Subsequently, a second complaint was lodged in Udaipur containing the same allegations as the first FIR.
The second complaint filed in Udaipur explicitly mentioned that an earlier complaint had already been lodged in Hisar.

The High Court dismissed the appellant's petition to quash the second FIR, finding that the Udaipur complaint was filed prior in time and that the Rajasthan Police were unaware of the Hisar proceedings.
law: Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, grants High Courts the inherent power to quash criminal proceedings to prevent abuse of the process of law or to secure the ends of justice.
application: The Supreme Court examined the two primary grounds on which the High Court based its decision and found them to be factually incorrect and contradictory to the record.
First, the Supreme Court noted that the High Court's finding that the Udaipur complaint was 'prior in point of time' was contrary to the admitted facts and records of the case.

Second, the Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in observing that the Rajasthan Police were unaware of the earlier proceedings. The record clearly showed that the Udaipur complaint itself mentioned the prior complaint lodged at Hisar, meaning the investigating agency was 'well aware' of it.
The Supreme Court concluded that these contradictory findings demonstrated a non-application of mind by the High Court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the High Court had erred on both counts by making findings that were contrary to the record and admitted facts. Therefore, the Supreme Court accepted the appellant's contention and found that the High Court was wrong to dismiss the petition to quash the second FIR.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in not quashing FIR under Section 482 of Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 in a complaint alleging offences under Sections 498A, 406, 384, 420, and 120(B), Indian Penal Code, 1860, on the ground that the second FIR was on the same set of allegations.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's counsel drew the court's attention to both complaints to show they were based on the same allegations.

The appellant relied on the legal precedents set in T.T. Antony v. State of Kerala & Ors. and Y. Abraham Ajith & Ors. v. Inspector of Police, Chennai & Anr. to argue against the maintainability of a second FIR on the same facts.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's counsel opposed the quashing of the FIR, relying on the precedent set in Prem Chand Singh v. State of UP.

arguments.issue_text: Non-application of mind by High Court – Findings of the High Court contradictory to the record and admitted facts.
appellant_arguments: The High Court's order contained errors apparent on the face of the record.

The High Court's findings were factually incorrect, specifically that the complaint at Udaipur was prior in time to the one at Hisar, and that the Rajasthan Police had no knowledge of the prior proceedings at Hisar.
respondent_arguments: The provided text does not specify the respondent's arguments on this issue.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A High Court's decision is erroneous when its findings are contradictory to the record and admitted facts, demonstrating a non-application of mind.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred on two counts. First, the High Court's finding that the second complaint (at Udaipur) was prior in time was contrary to the records and admitted facts, demonstrating a non-application of mind. Second, the complainant's conduct of filing a second FIR on the same allegations without withdrawing the first complaint or taking steps to transfer it constituted an abuse of the process of law, as it showed an intention to harass the appellant.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied the principle that a second FIR based on the same set of allegations is not maintainable.
The court assessed whether the complainant's actions constituted an 'abuse of process of law' under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which would justify quashing the FIR.
policy_considerations: The court identified the complainant's conduct—neither appearing before the trial court at Hisar nor withdrawing their complaint while filing another elsewhere—as evidence of an intention to harass the appellant, which constitutes a misuse of state machinery for ulterior motives.

The inaction of a complainant in either withdrawing a first complaint or seeking its transfer to the appropriate jurisdiction before filing a second complaint on the same facts is considered an abuse of the legal process.
